short: How far a poll's number could be from the true number just because the poll talked to a sample of people instead of everyone. A ±3 point margin on 50% means the real number is probably between 47% and 53%.
sports: Like a close play at the plate: if the lead is inside the margin of error, the poll can't say for sure who's ahead.

term: Margin of error on the lead
short: The gap between two candidates is less certain than either candidate's number alone, roughly twice the poll's stated margin of error. That's why a 4-point lead in a ±3 poll can still be a toss-up.
sports: Think of the lead as a score that could be off by a few points either way, like a replay that could go either way.

short: People the pollster thinks will actually vote, based on questions like past voting and interest. Each pollster decides this differently.
sports: The players expected to actually suit up on game day.

short: Everyone registered to vote, whether or not they're likely to show up.
sports: Everyone on the roster, including people who may not play on game day.

short: All adults, including people who aren't registered to vote. The least precise group for predicting an election.
sports: Everyone in the stadium, not just the players.

short: How many people answered the poll. More people means a smaller margin of error, but only if they were picked well.
sports: How many games are in the sample. More games gives you a better read on a team.

short: Adjusting poll answers so the group of people who answered matches the population (for example, by age, race, education or past vote). Every pollster weights differently.
sports: Like adjusting stats for strength of schedule so the sample matches the real league.

short: When one pollster's results lean in the same direction compared with other polls, again and again. It doesn't mean the pollster is wrong, just consistently different.
sports: A scorekeeper who always seems a little generous to one side.

short: When pollsters adjust or hold back results so they look like other polls. It can make polls look more certain than they are.
sports: Analysts all copying each other's picks instead of making their own.

short: A poll paid for by a campaign, a party, or a group that supports one side. It can still be accurate, but sponsors can choose which results to release.
sports: A stat sheet put out by one of the teams. It might be right, but they choose which stats to share.

short: Combining several polls into one number, which usually beats any single poll. Our formula is published on the Show Our Work page.
sports: The score. It combines many polls into one number, like a team's average across many games.

short: An expert forecaster's call on how competitive a race is, from Solid (not competitive) to Likely, Lean and Toss-up (anyone's race).
sports: Expert picks, like analysts predicting a game before it's played.

short: A race either side could realistically win. On our poll charts, it also means the margin-of-error range includes a tie.
sports: A coin-flip game: either side could realistically win.

short: The person who currently holds the seat.
sports: The defending champion: the person who holds the seat now.

short: The Federal Election Commission, the government agency that collects fundraising and spending reports from federal candidates.
How much money a campaign had in the bank at the end of its latest report.
sports: Money still in the bank, like a team's remaining budget.

short: Donations from people who gave $200 or less in total this cycle. Campaigns don't have to report these donors' names, so we can't see where they live.
Political action committee: a group that collects money and gives it to candidates, with legal limits on how much.
A group that can raise and spend unlimited money to support or oppose candidates, but isn't allowed to coordinate with campaigns.
sports: A booster club that can spend unlimited money but isn't allowed to coordinate with the team.

short: Money spent by groups other than the campaign itself (like super PACs) to help or hurt a candidate.
sports: Money spent by booster clubs, not by the team itself.

short: A ballot kept separate until election officials confirm you're eligible. It counts once they do.
A ballot mailed to you so you don't have to vote in person. In Virginia anyone registered can ask for one, no reason needed.
Redrawing the lines of voting districts, usually every 10 years after the census. Where the lines go can change which party is favored.
An outside expert a court appoints to do a specific job, like drawing a district map.

FiveThirtyEight's score for how accurate and open a pollster has been in past elections, from 0 to 3 (3 is best). Their ratings were last updated in September 2024, so newer pollsters may not have one.
sports: A scouting report on the pollster's track record.

short: How far the final polls were from the actual result, and in which direction. If polls showed a Democrat up 5 and they won by 1, polls overstated Democrats by 4 points.
sports: How far the final polls were from the real result, like a point spread that missed.

short: Our polling average for this race: each candidate's average share across recent checked polls. It's a poll average, not a result. Nobody has won anything until votes are counted.
sports: The score in the middle of the game. It can still change.

short: How many checked polls of this race came out in the last 60 days. More polls usually means a steadier average.
sports: Games played so far this season.

short: Who led each of the last five checked polls, newest first. Blue = Democrat, red = Republican, teal = another candidate, gray = tied.
sports: A team's recent form, like W-W-L-W-L.

short: The average rating from three forecasters: Cook Political Report, Inside Elections, and Sabato's Crystal Ball.
sports: Analysts' picks before the game.

short: At least one recent poll hasn't been checked against its original source yet, so we don't show a score until it is.
sports: The play is under review. The score waits until the replay is checked.

short: One candidate's lead in our average is bigger than a typical polling miss (about 4.6 points). It's still not a guarantee.
sports: Up by more than a couple of scores, but the game isn't over.
